documents.title: Artificial intelligence resources for faculty
documents.stance_why: The page itself sets no single rule: it asks faculty to "define permitted and prohibited use in your courses" and offers three sample syllabus statements (all use permitted with acknowledgment, limited use, no use), so the decision is delegated and the tiers are listed.
tiers: All use of generative AI is permitted, with acknowledgment
Limited use of generative AI is permitted in specific contexts
No use of generative AI tools permitted
documents.summary: The Provost's faculty page encourages faculty to learn about and experiment with generative AI, asks them to state permitted and prohibited uses in the syllabus, and supplies three sample statements. It warns that detectors are not definitive evidence, says not to mandate AI use, and restricts sharing sensitive data.

units.why: The overview says NAU "encourages faculty to stay informed about the latest advancements in artificial intelligence", a recommendation to instructors to learn about AI; P63 is nearest.
units.anchor: encourages faculty to stay informed about the latest advancements in artificial intelligence
units.fit_note: P63 is about workshops and support; this is a plain encouragement to stay informed.

units.why: Faculty are told to "guide students in using AI as a supportive resource rather than a substitute for critical thinking and learning", about keeping students as the thinkers, so P32.
units.anchor: guide students in using AI as a supportive resource rather than a substitute

units.why: Instructors are directed to "Provide and discuss clear syllabus policy statements that define permitted and prohibited use", a duty to state AI expectations in the syllabus, so P09.
units.anchor: Provide and discuss clear syllabus policy statements that define permitted and prohibited use

units.why: The university offers "sample syllabi statements to use as a starting point", developed with instructional designers; this is support for instructors in setting policy, nearest P63.
units.anchor: we offer sample syllabi statements to use as a starting point
units.policy: The university offers sample syllabi statements developed with instructional designers as a starting point, which may be modified to fit specific course or assignment needs.
units.fit_note: P63 covers workshops and advice; this is provision of ready-made template wording.

units.why: "Unauthorized uses of GenAI, as defined by the instructor, may constitute an academic integrity violation" classifies unauthorized AI use as misconduct (P36) while leaving the definition to instructors; P36 chosen over P04 because the sentence is about consequence.
units.anchor: Unauthorized uses of GenAI, as defined by the instructor, may constitute an academic integrity violation

units.why: "Do not mandate student use" is an explicit rule that instructors not require AI, citing "undue burden"; this is the equity type P51.
units.anchor: Do not mandate student use
units.fit_note: The heading states a prohibition on requiring AI; the text gives accessibility and personal concerns as reasons.

units.why: "Faculty should provide a non-GenAI option for students when incorporating these tools" is an alternative-access rule, so P51.
units.anchor: Faculty should provide a non-GenAI option for students

units.why: Detectors "are imperfect and may return false positives and false negatives", so they should not be relied on; P39, while the evidence-standard sentence is coded separately as P69.
units.anchor: are imperfect and may return false positives and false negatives

units.why: "results such detectors produce cannot be considered as definitive evidence of an academic integrity violation" sets what is not enough evidence for a finding, so P69 rather than P39.
units.anchor: cannot be considered as definitive evidence of an academic integrity violation

units.why: Faculty are invited to "outline schedules and topics for new modules or lessons, or generate variations of exam questions", instructor AI use for teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: Explore using generative AI to outline schedules and topics for new modules or lessons

units.why: Suggests asking "students to explore a high-level topic using GenAI chatbots and report their detailed findings", AI used to learn a topic, P12.
units.anchor: Ask students to explore a high-level topic using GenAI chatbots
units.fit_note: Also asks students to report their findings, a course-assigned use rather than only tutoring.

units.why: Suggests students "create their own practice exams by generating questions on key course topics", a practice and study-aid use, P14.
units.anchor: create their own practice exams by generating questions on key course topics

units.why: Suggests students "create and refine outlines and first drafts of writing assignments" with AI, a prose-specific use, P18.
units.anchor: create and refine outlines and first drafts of writing assignments

units.why: "Seek opportunities to make curricular changes that build on the changes you anticipate" because AI has "augmented the standard toolkits in many occupations" ties AI to professional preparation, P44.
units.anchor: Seek opportunities to make curricular changes that build on the changes you anticipate

units.why: The TRAIL program with grants "to support faculty in developing innovative approaches for applying AI technologies" is institutional support for faculty experimenting with AI, P63.
units.anchor: aims to support faculty in developing innovative approaches for applying AI technologies
units.policy: The TRAIL program, launching in academic year 2024-2025 with grants, aims to support faculty in developing innovative approaches for applying AI technologies to student learning and the broader educational enterprise.

units.why: The first sample statement says the course "allows the use of generative AI for any work submitted", a permit-by-default stance, P02.
units.anchor: allows the use of generative AI for any work submitted by students

units.why: "there is an expectation to acknowledge what content was generated by generative AI tools" requires disclosure with a submission, P24.
units.anchor: there is an expectation to acknowledge what content was generated by generative AI tools
units.fit_note: Also gives example formats (different colored font, direct quote, parenthetical citation).

units.why: "please ask for clarification before submitting assignments" tells students unsure how to acknowledge to ask first, P10.
units.anchor: please ask for clarification before submitting assignments
units.fit_note: Asking is about how to acknowledge AI use, not whether a use is allowed.

units.why: The second sample statement allows AI "as part of the research and preparation phase", for ideas, summaries and drafts that feed the student's own work; nearest P15.
units.anchor: as part of the research and preparation phase of the work
units.fit_note: Covers research, idea generation, topic summaries and draft text as input, limited to the preparation phase.

units.why: Students "should critically evaluate the sources, methods, and outputs of generative AI systems" because information "is not always reliable or accurate": verify AI output, P31.
units.anchor: should critically evaluate the sources, methods, and outputs of generative AI systems
units.frag_start: In this use, students should be

units.why: "Any final work submitted by students ... is expected to be generated by the students themselves" bars AI producing the submitted work, P19.
units.anchor: is expected to be generated by the students themselves

units.why: "Submitting final work created by generative AI constitutes an academic integrity violation" classifies it as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: Submitting final work created by generative AI constitutes an academic integrity violation

units.why: "if you are unsure whether a particular use of generative AI is acceptable, please ask for clarification before using" is the ask-first rule, P10.
units.anchor: if you are unsure whether a particular use of generative AI is acceptable
units.frag_start: If you have any questions about this

units.why: The third sample statement says all submitted work "including all process work, drafts, brainstorming artifacts, and final work" is generated "entirely by the students themselves": a ban for the course, P01.
units.anchor: including all process work, drafts, brainstorming artifacts, and final work

units.why: "Any use of generative artificial intelligence tools, such as ChatGPT, constitutes an academic integrity violation" ties any use to misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: Any use of generative artificial intelligence tools, such as ChatGPT, constitutes an academic integrity violation

units.why: "NAU faculty members have access to Copilot ... at no cost" describes a licensed institution-provided AI tool, P17.
units.anchor: NAU faculty members have access to Copilot

units.why: Extended Copilot licensing is available "For $400 per year", a paid tier offered through the university; nearest P17.
units.anchor: For $400 per year, extended licensing is available for Microsoft Copilot
units.fit_note: Describes a paid extended license faculty can obtain, not a free sanctioned tool.

units.why: "never share any sensitive data" with generative AI tools "even those supported by NAU" is a data protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: even those supported by NAU, never share any sensitive data.

units.why: "Any data above a level 2 classification ... should not be shared with generative AI tools" specifies the threshold for data that must stay out of AI, P50.
units.anchor: should not be shared with generative AI tools

documents.title: Artificial intelligence resources for students
documents.stance_why: AI use is encouraged only "when approved by faculty" and "guidelines for generative AI may differ between courses, depending on instructor preferences", so the page sets no stance of its own and hands the decision to instructors.
documents.summary: The student page encourages responsible AI use in coursework only when faculty approve and tells students to check the syllabus or ask. It bars using AI to write posts, essays or answers, asks students to verify output, protect sensitive data, and describes alternatives and accessibility options.

units.why: "NAU encourages students to stay informed" because AI "may play a significant role in their future careers" links AI awareness to professional preparation, P44.
units.anchor: these tools may play a significant role in their future careers

units.why: Students should use AI "as an effective companion rather than relying on it entirely", keeping the student as the main problem-solver, P32.
units.anchor: as an effective companion rather than relying on it entirely
units.frag_start: as well as how to utilize

units.why: "NAU encourages the responsible and ethical use of AI in coursework when approved by faculty" makes faculty approval the condition, so the decision sits with instructors, P04.
units.anchor: encourages the responsible and ethical use of AI in coursework when approved by faculty

units.why: "guidelines for generative AI may differ between courses, depending on instructor preferences" says rules are course-specific, P11.
units.anchor: guidelines for generative AI may differ between courses, depending on instructor preferences

units.why: "it's essential to check your course syllabus for any guidelines related to generative AI tools" tells students to look up the rule before using AI; closest is P10 as no type covers checking the syllabus.

units.frag_start: Before using AI in your coursework
units.fit_note: P10 is about asking; this tells students to check the syllabus before using AI.

units.why: "If AI isn't explicitly mentioned, ask your instructor for clarification" is an ask-first rule when the syllabus is silent, P10 rather than P06 because no fallback rule is stated.
units.anchor: ask your instructor for clarification

units.why: "aim to use them as a way to enhance your learning or efficiency, not as a shortcut for producing answers or original work" keeps AI from replacing the student's work, P32.

units.why: "Don't use AI to write your discussion posts, essays, or answer questions on your behalf" bans AI producing submitted work, P19.

units.why: "always verify information with a trusted source" because AI "may produce incorrect information" is verification of output, P31.
units.anchor: always verify information with a trusted source

units.why: "Using generative AI tools when prohibited can lead to disciplinary action and may result in an academic integrity violation" states misuse consequences, P36.
units.anchor: can lead to disciplinary action and may result in an academic integrity violation
units.frag_start: Using generative AI tools when prohibited

units.why: "If your instructor has set guidelines against using AI in your coursework, always respect their policy" makes the instructor's rule binding, P04.

units.why: "Don't use AI to replace your genuine responses and original thoughts" in discussion and replies keeps students as the thinkers, P32; P58 is for messages to course staff, which this is not.
units.anchor: Don't use AI to replace your genuine responses and original thoughts.

units.why: "instructors are encouraged to offer alternative options for any assignments or tasks that involve AI" is an alternatives rule for equity, P51.

documents.title: AI and Acceptable Use
documents.stance_why: AI use is allowed under conditions: users must "use your NAU credentials", stay the "final decision-maker", respect FERPA and HIPAA, and use "Lean AI" practices; nothing bans or requires AI, so permit with conditions.
documents.summary: The ITS page says AI use is governed by the existing Appropriate Use of IT Resources policy rather than new rules. It lists principles: users remain responsible for AI output, must use NAU credentials, respect privacy and IP laws, and use efficient tools.

units.why: "Use of Artificial Intelligence at Northern Arizona University is governed by our" existing policy, with no separate rules, P77.
units.anchor: Use of Artificial Intelligence at Northern Arizona University is governed by our

units.why: "Every output generated by an AI tool is your professional responsibility" and the user is "the final decision-maker", so the person owns the output, P29.
units.anchor: Every output generated by an AI tool is your professional responsibility

units.why: "you must use your NAU credentials for all university-related AI tasks" is a vetted-tool and data protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: you must use your NAU credentials for all university-related AI tasks
units.frag_start: To ensure your data is protected

units.why: "Inputting sensitive university data into unapproved or personal AI accounts is a violation of our security standards" classifies a data practice as a violation, P50.
units.anchor: Inputting sensitive university data into unapproved or personal AI accounts is a violation

units.why: "Treat AI as a collaborator, not a replacement" keeps the human as the primary worker, P32; P45 (like a human collaborator under existing rules) is not stated here.
units.anchor: Treat AI as a collaborator, not a replacement.

units.why: "Always respect data security policy, student privacy (FERPA), health data (HIPAA)" requires following law and policy, P77.
units.anchor: student privacy (FERPA), health data (HIPAA), and the intellectual property of your colleagues

units.why: "we encourage “Lean AI” practices. Only use the most efficient tool for the task to minimize the environmental footprint" raises environmental cost, P53.
units.anchor: Only use the most efficient tool for the task to minimize the environmental footprint
